sections.text: Two small traits give smart pointers their special feel. Deref controls what the * operator does. Drop lets you run code when a value goes away. You already know the idea of * from references: it follows the reference to get the value it points at. A Box works the same way.

You can make your own type behave like that by implementing the Deref trait. Below is a tiny box type called MyBox. struct MyBox<T>(T); is a tuple struct: a struct with unnamed fields, here one field of any type T, which you reach as .0. The Deref trait needs two things. type Target = T; says what type * gives back (this is called an associated type). The method deref returns a reference to that inner value.

The last line shows deref coercion. hello wants a &str, but we pass &MyBox<String>. Rust sees that MyBox implements Deref, so it calls deref to get a &String, and String implements Deref too, so it goes one more step to get a &str. All of this happens at compile time, with no cost at run time. It is why you can pass &String where &str is expected, and why the &Box<List> in the last lesson worked where a &List was expected.

Now Drop. If a type implements Drop, Rust calls its drop method automatically when a value goes out of scope. That's the place to close a file, release a lock, or print a message. You never write the cleanup call yourself.

Read the output, shown in the comment at the end of the code, from the top. temp is dropped at the closing brace of its block. early is dropped by the call to drop(early). At the end of main, the remaining values are dropped in the reverse order of creation: second first, then first. So the last value created is the first one cleaned up.

To clean up early, call the function drop(value). It is in Rust's prelude, so you don't need a use line. It takes the value by ownership, so after drop(early) you can't use early any more. Calling the method yourself, early.drop(), is not allowed. This code does not compile. Rust reports E0040: explicit use of destructor method. The reason is that Rust would call drop again at the end of the scope, and cleaning up twice would be a bug.

Think of Drop as a to-do list item that Rust ticks off for you: "when this thing goes out of scope, do this". Because it is automatic, you can't forget to clean up. You saw the same idea earlier: when a String goes out of scope, its memory is freed. Drop is how that happens.

Coming from C++: Drop is the destructor, and the reverse-order cleanup is RAII, just as in C++. Java's try-with-resources, C#'s using and Python's with give deterministic cleanup for one block. Rust does it for every value automatically, with no special syntax. Java finalizers, by contrast, may run late or never, and are deprecated for removal. Deref also has a sibling, DerefMut, for *x on a mutable value. Fields of a struct are dropped after the struct's own drop, in the order they were declared. This is the opposite of C++, which destroys members in reverse order.

exercise.prompt: Right now first is dropped at the very end of main. Change the program so first is cleaned up before the line that prints working, while second stays alive until the end. It should print four lines: guards: first and second, dropping first, working, dropping second. Hint: call drop(first); just before println!("working").
exercise.expectedOutput:
guards: first and second
dropping first
working
dropping second

quiz.question: In what order does Rust drop local variables at the end of a scope?
options: In the order they were created, first created dropped first
In reverse order of creation, last created dropped first
In alphabetical order of the variable names

quiz.question: What does implementing the Deref trait customize?
options: How a value is printed when you use {}
How a value is copied when you assign it
What the * operator gives back for the value

quiz.question: How do you clean up a value before the end of its scope?
options: Call value.drop(), the method on the value
Set the variable to None so it is released
